title: Evelyn
full_review:
A father whose children have been legally taken from him after his wife runs off takes on the system in 1950s' Ireland in the heartfelt, fact-based drama "Evelyn" (MGM). The film is a labor of love for Irish-born Pierce Brosnan, who produced as well as starred in a role light years away from his suave James Bond persona.

It's not a very happy Christmas in 1953 Dublin with housepainter dad Desmond (Brosnan) out of work. But matters get infinitely worse when young daughter Evelyn (Sophie Vavasseur) sees her mom, suitcase in hand, drive off with a strange man, never to be heard from again.

Without steady employment, Desmond is at the mercy of the Children's Act of 1941 and the state sends Evelyn to an orphanage run by nuns while younger sons Dermot and Maurice go a Christian Brothers orphanage.

Devastated, Desmond spends his evenings at the local pub where the barmaid (Julianna Margulies) has him contact her solicitor brother Michael (Stephen Rea) for help. Desmond's widowed dad is supportive, singing at the pub with his son for a little income, and Desmond finds work once more.

However, the law requires the wife, who moved to Australia, address unknown, to sign off on allowing Desmond to reclaim his children. Not only does the judge rule against Desmond, but he forbids any appeal.

Meanwhile, nasty Sister Bridgett at the orphanage viciously slaps Evelyn, making Desmond more desperate to protect and win back his children. When Irish-American lawyer Nick (Aidan Quinn) and his retired mentor (Alan Bates) join the cause, they decide to take a new legal approach to the Supreme Court.

Although the film depicts one nun as brutal, the others are seen as kindly and caring (unlike the upcoming biased Miramax film "The Magdalene Sisters," in which every religious is a monster). Under Bruce Beresford's fine direction, it is the Children's Act of 1941 that is seen as clearly unfair in circumstances such as Desmond's.

Character-driven and with nicely nuanced performances all around, "Evelyn" has a lot of heart and a surprising amount of humor and wit, given the hardscrabble situations the characters experience. And most of all, one gets a sense of the faith of the Irish people. No one turns angrily against God when suffering comes. There are several scenes that affirm faith, such as when the prosecutor scorns Desmond as not being able to duplicate the Holy Family as the correct model for family life. His response, invoking instead the model of the Holy Trinity, is a marvel.

Desmond always believes that God will help him to win the case and then to help him raise his children just as God helped his father when his mother died at an early age. When little Evelyn is put on the stand and accused of lying about being beaten, she shows no bitterness toward the offending nun, only a wish not to get her in trouble -- and the hope that she goes to confession soon. This dry wit enlivens the movie on a regular basis and makes what could have been a glum downtrodden story a film of hope and humor. Even the fiery Alan Bates character, who claims to be an atheist, is revealed to be a believer when his rosary beads slip out of his pocket.

The film does indulge in a heavy religious sentimentality, however. Before he passes on, Evelyn's grandfather tells her the sun's rays shining on her hands as they talk at the orphanage are really angel rays meant to comfort and guide her. After his death, Evelyn believes the rays are a signal from her granddad that he is watching, and her wide-eyed explanation of this in court may smack of being a tad emotionally manipulative. Yet Vavasseur's performance captures a child's faith and optimistic innocence as the courtroom scenes build momentum toward a stirring conclusion.

Shot on location, the visuals are atmospheric and there is little difficulty understanding the Irish brogue. More important is how the themes of justice, familial love and faith are expressed so eloquently.

Neatly worked into the narrative as a charming subplot is a competitive romance when both Desmond and barrister Nick take an interest in barmaid Bernadette, who is influential in motivating Desmond to turn away from drink.

While Brosnan is excellent overall, as for his talent as a pub singer, 'tis better he keep his day job.

Due to fleeting violence, ill-gotten gambling gains and occasional profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
